answer.label: Not Victor Hugo — actually Herbert Kretzmer
answer.authorDates: 1925–2020 · South African-born British journalist, songwriter & lyricist
answer.sourceLine: This line is not from Victor Hugo's 1862 novel Les Misérables. It is the closing line of “Valjean's Death” in the 1985 stage musical, written by English lyricist Herbert Kretzmer, who adapted rather than translated Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel's French libretto.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: And remember, the truth that once was spoken: To love another person is to see the face of God.
trail: The line is sung by Valjean, Fantine, and Éponine in the “Valjean's Death” finale of the stage musical Les Misérables, per Wikiquote ↗.
English lyrics for the 1985 production were written by journalist-turned-lyricist Herbert Kretzmer, per Wikipedia ↗.

Kretzmer said he did not literally translate the French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel — he read Hugo's novel and a literal translation of the French text, then wrote substantial new material, per Bellingua Translations ↗.
The exact sentence is catalogued on Goodreads under Kretzmer's name and tagged to the musical, not to Hugo's novel, per Goodreads ↗.
source.excerptNote: Sung by Jean Valjean, Fantine, and Éponine as Valjean dies, in the musical's closing scene.
source.rightsHolder: Rights holders of the Les Misérables stage musical (Cameron Mackintosh Ltd. / Alain Boublil Music Ltd.) and the estate of Herbert Kretzmer
source.rightsNote: This line is a lyric from a 1985 stage musical still under copyright, not a passage from Hugo's public-domain 1862 novel. Rights belong to the show's producers and Kretzmer's estate, not to Victor Hugo.

author.name: Herbert Kretzmer
author.kicker: The real author of the wording
author.heading: About Herbert Kretzmer
author.metaLine: 1925–2020 · South African-born British journalist, songwriter & lyricist
author.bio: Kretzmer was a journalist and theatre critic who also wrote pop lyrics, including hits for Charles Aznavour. In 1985 producer Cameron Mackintosh commissioned him, on short notice, to write the English-language libretto for the French musical Les Misérables. Kretzmer read Victor Hugo's novel and a literal translation of the French show, then wrote substantial new English lyrics rather than a direct translation.

misattribution.intro: This is one of the most-searched “Victor Hugo quotes” online, but it never appears in Hugo's 1862 novel — it was written well over a century later, for the stage.

context.heading: How the line entered the world
lead: Search this quote and you'll get page after page crediting Victor Hugo. In reality it's the closing line of the Broadway/West End musical Les Misérables, sung by Jean Valjean, Fantine, and Éponine as Valjean dies and is received into the light.

The English libretto was written in 1985 by Herbert Kretzmer, a South African-born British journalist and songwriter who took over the project on short notice for producer Cameron Mackintosh. Kretzmer has said he worked from a literal translation of Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel's original French show, and from Hugo's novel itself, then wrote substantial new lyrics of his own rather than translating directly — which is exactly what happened at the finale.
detailsBody: Hugo's 1862 novel does share the musical's underlying theme — that love, mercy, and grace are how Jean Valjean glimpses the divine — but that theme is expressed across hundreds of pages of narrative and authorial digression, not in a single quotable sentence resembling this one.
context.pull: The words are Herbert Kretzmer's, written for the stage in 1985 — not Victor Hugo's, from the page in 1862.
